cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600 (as amended by SB 699, eff. Jan. 1, 2024)
proposition: Except as provided in the chapter, every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade or business is to that extent void; (b)(1) directs that the section be read broadly, in accordance with Edwards (2008), to void the application of any noncompete agreement in an employment context or noncompete clause in an employment contract, no matter how narrowly tailored, that does not satisfy an exception in the chapter; (b)(2) declares that subdivision is declaratory of, not a change in, existing law.

cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.5 (eff. Jan. 1, 2024)
proposition: (a) a contract void under the chapter is unenforceable regardless of where and when it was signed; (b) an employer or former employer shall not attempt to enforce a void contract regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment maintained outside California; (c) an employer shall not enter into a contract with an employee or prospective employee that includes a provision void under the chapter; (d) an employer that enters into or attempts to enforce a void contract commits a civil violation; (e)(1) an employee, former employee or prospective employee may bring a private action for injunctive relief or actual damages, or both, and (e)(2) a prevailing employee, former employee or prospective employee shall be entitled to reasonable attorney's fees and costs.

cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.1 (eff. Jan. 1, 2024)
proposition: (a) unlawful to include a noncompete clause in an employment contract, or to require an employee to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception in the chapter; (b)(1) for current employees, and for former employees who were employed after January 1, 2022, whose contracts include a noncompete clause, or who were required to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy a chapter exception, the employer shall, by February 14, 2024, notify the employee that the clause or agreement is void; (b)(2) notice shall be a written individualized communication to the employee or former employee, delivered to the last known address and the email address of the employee; (c) a violation is an act of unfair competition within the meaning of the Chapter 5 (starting with §17200) scheme.

cite: Cal. Lab. Code §925
proposition: Employer shall not require an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would (1) require the employee to adjudicate outside California a claim arising in California, or (2) deprive the employee of the substantive protection of California law for a controversy arising in California; a violating provision is voidable by the employee, and if rendered void at the employee's request the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern; a court may award the employee enforcing these rights reasonable attorney's fees; §925(e) does not apply to an employee in fact individually represented by legal counsel in negotiating the venue/forum or choice-of-law terms; applies to contracts entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2017.

cite: Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP, 44 Cal.4th 937 (2008)
proposition: Section 16600 voids noncompetition agreements in the employment context unless within a statutory exception; rejects the Ninth Circuit 'narrow restraint' exception; noncompetes are invalid even if narrowly drawn; disapproves Campbell and General Commercial Packaging to the extent inconsistent.

cite: Campbell v. Board of Trustees of Leland Stanford Junior University, 817 F.2d 499 (9th Cir. 1987)
proposition: Ninth Circuit applied a 'narrow restraint' exception under which a restraint barring an employee from only a small or limited part of the business, trade or profession does not violate §16600; the library records that this reasoning was rejected by Edwards v. Arthur Andersen (2008) and that the narrow-restraint exception is not California law.

cite: General Commercial Packaging, Inc. v. TPS Package Engineering, Inc., 126 F.3d 1131 (9th Cir. 1997)
proposition: Ninth Circuit upheld a contractual provision as a 'narrow restraint' not barred by §16600; the library records that it was disapproved in Edwards (2008).

cite: FTC Non-Compete Clause Rule, 16 C.F.R. pt. 910, 89 Fed. Reg. 38342 (May 7, 2024)
proposition: The Rule would have declared most worker non-compete clauses an unfair method of competition and required notice to workers; the library records that it was set aside nationwide in Ryan LLC v. FTC (N.D. Tex. Aug. 20, 2024), that the FTC voted in September 2025 to dismiss its appeal and accede to vacatur, and that the Rule never took effect and is not in force.
status_checked: vacated — see Ryan LLC v. FTC

cite: Ryan LLC v. Federal Trade Commission, 739 F. Supp. 3d 496 (N.D. Tex. 2024)
proposition: FTC lacked substantive rulemaking authority under FTC Act §6(g) and the Rule was arbitrary and capricious; Rule set aside with nationwide APA effect; Fifth Circuit appeal voluntarily dismissed September 2025.

§15.50(a): a covenant not to compete is enforceable if it is ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement at the time the agreement is made, and then only to the extent its limitations as to time, geographical area and scope of activity are reasonable and impose no greater restraint than is necessary to protect the goodwill or other business interest of the promisee. §15.51(b): in an action to enforce, the promisee bears the burden on §15.50(a) if the primary purpose of the agreement is to obligate the promisor to render personal services. §15.51(c): if the limitations are unreasonable the court shall reform the covenant to the extent necessary and enforce it as reformed, but may not award damages for breach before reformation. §15.52: the §15.51 procedures and remedies are exclusive and preempt any other criteria for enforceability under common law or otherwise.

cite: Alex Sheshunoff Management Services, L.P. v. Johnson, 209 S.W.3d 644 (Tex. 2006)
proposition: A covenant in an at-will employment agreement is enforceable where the employer's promise (e.g., to provide confidential information) is performed, even if not performed at the moment of contracting; modifies Light's timing requirement; the core inquiry is reasonableness under §15.50.

cite: Light v. Centel Cellular Co. of Texas, 883 S.W.2d 642 (Tex. 1994)
proposition: Cited only for its status note: it held a covenant must be ancillary to an otherwise enforceable agreement and set out a two-part test requiring that the consideration be given, and the covenant be designed to enforce the employee's return promise, at the time the agreement is made; the library records that the timing requirement was overruled/modified by Sheshunoff (2006) and that Light should not be cited for the proposition that a unilateral at-will agreement cannot support a covenant.

cite: Marsh USA Inc. v. Cook, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011)
proposition: Stock options granted to a managing director were reasonably related to the employer's interest in protecting goodwill and could support a covenant not to compete; the Court rejected a narrow 'give rise' requirement for the consideration.

cite: DeSantis v. Wackenhut Corp., 793 S.W.2d 670 (Tex. 1990)
proposition: Applying Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187, the Texas Supreme Court refused to apply a Florida choice-of-law clause to a non-compete for an employee working in Texas, because Texas had a materially greater interest and application of Florida law would contravene fundamental Texas policy on non-competes; a choice-of-law clause does not control the enforceability of a non-compete where the state with the materially greater interest has a fundamental contrary policy.

cite: Nedlloyd Lines B.V. v. Superior Court, 3 Cal.4th 459 (1992)
proposition: California follows Restatement §187: chosen law enforced if the chosen state has a substantial relationship, unless contrary to a fundamental California policy and California has a materially greater interest in the issue.

cite: Application Group, Inc. v. Hunter Group, Inc., 61 Cal.App.4th 881 (1998)
proposition: California had a materially greater interest in applying §16600 to a Maryland employer's noncompete with an employee recruited to work for a California employer; the out-of-state choice-of-law clause did not control; California's policy against noncompetes is 'fundamental.'

cite: Advanced Bionics Corp. v. Medtronic, Inc., 29 Cal.4th 697 (2002)
proposition: Addressing parallel California and Minnesota litigation over a non-compete, the Court held California courts should generally not enjoin a party from pursuing litigation in another state's courts, reversing a TRO, and cautioned about interstate forum conflicts; it does not retreat from §16600's policy.

cite: Ixchel Pharma, LLC v. Biogen, Inc., 9 Cal.5th 1130 (2020)
proposition: A rule of reason applies to §16600 challenges to restraints in business-to-business contracts; the Court distinguished the employment context, where Edwards governs and non-competes are void.

cite: Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187(2)
proposition: Chosen law applies unless the chosen state has no substantial relationship/reasonable basis, or application would be contrary to a fundamental policy of a state with a materially greater interest that would be the applicable-law state under §188 absent the choice. (§188's text is not in the library.)

cite: Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §17.042; Michiana Easy Livin' Country v. Holten, 168 S.W.3d 777 (Tex. 2005) (library practice note)
proposition: A Travis County forum clause generally supplies consent to personal jurisdiction, but if the clause is voided under Cal. Lab. Code §925 at the employee's election the Texas court must find independent minimum contacts, and two short Austin trips plus a contract with a Texas employer 'may or may not' suffice; a Texas injunction would face non-recognition in California on public-policy grounds.
